blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
British irony is not just about jokes. At the intermediate level, you start to notice how much of daily conversation is carried on half-ironic. "Oh, brilliant," said flatly about a problem, actually means 'this is bad'. "Well, that's one way to do it," usually means 'I would have done it very differently'. And "He's not entirely wrong" is a cautious way of saying 'he is right'.

Understatement is the close cousin of irony. "Bit of a nightmare" may describe a genuinely terrible day. "Rather cold outside" may mean snow up to your knees. "Somewhat disappointing" may describe a total failure. The words stay small on purpose, while the reality behind them is anything but.

Learning to hear these signals is like learning a dialect. Once you can, you unlock a lot of what is really being said in a British office — and why people who do not hear it often feel confused by the mood of the room.

items.q: According to the text, when someone says "Oh, brilliant" flatly about a problem, they mean…
items.why: "'Oh, brilliant,' said flatly about a problem, actually means 'this is bad'."

items.q: How does the text describe understatement?
items.why: "Understatement is the close cousin of irony."

items.q: The text compares learning to hear these signals to…
items.why: "Learning to hear these signals is like learning a dialect."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: British colleagues often mean more than they literally say.
Missing these signals can make a meeting confusing.
You should take "rather cold outside" at face value.
Tone and context change the meaning of ordinary words.
items.why: Inferência: o texto inteiro alerta que 'rather cold' pode ser neve até o joelho — tomar ao pé da letra é o erro.

items.q: The phrase "the reality behind them is anything but" suggests that…
options: the speaker is not being honest
the situation is exactly as small as the words say
the words are much milder than what really happened
items.why: Inferência: 'anything but [small]' = a realidade é tudo menos pequena; as palavras minimizam algo grave.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Oliver explicando a um colega novo. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So, you looked a bit lost in that meeting just now. Let me help you decode it. When the manager leaned back and said the launch had been 'a bit of a nightmare' — very calm, almost cheerful — that was not calm at all. In plain English, the project had completely fallen apart. Missed deadline, angry client, the lot.

Here's the thing. The calmer a British manager sounds, the worse it often is. If he'd been genuinely relaxed, he might have said it went 'not bad'. And 'not bad', by the way, usually means it went rather well. I know, it makes no sense on paper.

Watch the small words too. 'Somewhat disappointing numbers' means the numbers are frankly awful. 'Rather tight timeline' means there is basically no time at all. The word stays tiny; the problem is huge.

My advice? Don't take any of it literally for the first few weeks. Listen for the pause, the flat tone, the little smile. Once you catch the pattern, you'll understand the real mood of the room — and you'll stop being the only person who thinks everything is fine.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What did the manager's calm 'a bit of a nightmare' actually mean?
options: The project had completely fallen apart
There was a minor delay only
The manager was relaxed and happy
items.why: "the project had completely fallen apart. Missed deadline, angry client, the lot."

items.q: According to Oliver, what does 'not bad' usually mean?
items.why: "'not bad'… usually means it went rather well."

items.q: What does Oliver say about 'somewhat disappointing numbers'?
options: The numbers are still being counted
The numbers are slightly below target
items.why: "'Somewhat disappointing numbers' means the numbers are frankly awful."

items.q: What does Oliver imply with "the calmer a British manager sounds, the worse it often is"?
options: Managers rarely discuss problems at all
You should trust a manager's surface tone
A relaxed tone can hide a serious problem
items.why: Inferência: o tom tranquilo pode ser justamente o sinal de que a situação é grave.

items.q: Why does Oliver tell the colleague not to take things literally at first?
options: Because British people rarely speak in meetings
Because the manager was joking about everything
Because the colleague might otherwise misread the real mood of the room
items.why: Inferência: sem captar o padrão, o colega seria 'the only person who thinks everything is fine'.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "He answered flatly, without any warmth in his voice." Flatly means…
items.why: Flatly = em tom seco, sem emoção — o sinal clássico da ironia britânica.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "The results were ___ disappointing, which for a Brit probably means a real failure."
items.why: Somewhat = um tanto: forma diplomática de dizer 'muito'.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "It's ___ cold in here — I can barely feel my hands."
items.why: Rather = bastante; sinaliza algo mais forte do que parece.

items.q: "Once you learn to read the signals, you unlock what is really being said." To unlock here means to…
items.why: To unlock = destravar; acessar o sentido que estava escondido.

items.q: "Newcomers often misread the mood of the room." This phrase refers to…
options: the layout of the meeting space
the overall feeling or atmosphere among the people present
items.why: Mood of the room = o clima, o estado de ânimo geral das pessoas presentes.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs comuns em reuniões. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The client feedback was polite, but I could tell they were pushing back on the price." To push back on means to…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar de algo, ainda que educadamente.

items.q: "When a Brit says 'not bad', try to read between the lines." To read between the lines means to…
options: understand the hidden or implied meaning
items.why: Read between the lines = entender o que está implícito, não apenas o literal.

items.q: "Their 'somewhat disappointing' comment was really a watered-down way of saying 'terrible'." Watered-down means…
items.why: Watered-down = suavizado, enfraquecido — exatamente o que o understatement faz.

items.q: "Don't take it at face value when a manager sounds calm about a crisis." To take something at face value means to…
options: accept it literally, as it appears
items.why: Take at face value = aceitar ao pé da letra — o erro que a lição alerta a evitar.

items.q: "It took me weeks to get the hang of British understatement." To get the hang of means to…
options: learn how to do or understand something
items.why: Get the hang of = pegar o jeito, aprender a lidar com algo.
